lesson.title: Gold, Silver, and the Fight Over the Value of a Dollar
lesson.summary: For much of the late 1800s, Americans fought bitterly over what should back the nation's money, pitting debt burdened farmers who wanted cheaper, more plentiful silver currency against bankers and creditors who defended the gold standard.
lesson.body:
For most of the nineteenth century the United States operated on a bimetallic standard, coining both gold and silver. That changed with the Coinage Act of 1873, which quietly ended the Treasury's coinage of silver dollars and put the country on a de facto gold standard. Silver advocates later dubbed this law the "Crime of '73," accusing bankers and creditors of engineering the change to their own benefit, though historians generally see it as a less deliberate, more bureaucratic decision that nonetheless had enormous consequences. The debate echoed an older fight over centralized financial power: decades earlier, President Andrew Jackson had killed the Second Bank of the United States, convinced that concentrated financial institutions served elite creditors at the expense of ordinary debtors, and that same suspicion of concentrated monetary power ran straight through the free silver debate of the 1890s.

The stakes were concrete. Gold was scarcer than silver, so tying the currency strictly to gold limited how fast the money supply could grow, even as the American economy and population were expanding rapidly. A limited money supply chasing a growing economy produced deflation, meaning each dollar bought more over time. Deflation benefited creditors, banks and bondholders who collected fixed payments worth more in real terms, but it devastated debtors, especially farmers who had borrowed to buy land and equipment and now had to repay those loans in dollars worth more than the ones they had originally borrowed, all while crop prices kept falling.

The free silver movement demanded that the government resume unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed ratio of sixteen ounces of silver to one ounce of gold. This would have expanded the money supply, produced mild inflation, made debts easier to repay, and likely lifted crop prices. Congress passed partial measures, most notably the Sherman Silver Purchase Act of 1890, which required the Treasury to buy large amounts of silver without fully restoring free coinage. President Grover Cleveland, a committed gold standard Democrat, pushed for the act's repeal in 1893 amid a severe economic downturn known as the Panic of 1893, a move that infuriated silver Democrats within his own party.

William Jennings Bryan made free silver the defining issue of his 1896 presidential campaign, and his Cross of Gold speech was a direct assault on gold standard orthodoxy. His defeat, combined with new gold discoveries in Alaska and South Africa later in the 1890s that eased the money supply naturally, drained much of the urgency from the debate. The Gold Standard Act of 1900, signed into law by President McKinley, formally and permanently committed the United States currency to gold, closing a fight that had dominated American politics for a generation.
